--- title: "Model Fitting and Interpretation" subtitle: "Introduction to Global Health Data Science" date: "2026-10-19" format: revealjs: output-file: w08-02-fitting-interpretation-slides.html footer: "[🔗 sta198-fa26-2.github.io](https://sta198-fa26-2.github.io/)" theme: slides.scss transition: fade slide-number: true pdf-separate-fragments: true toc: false html: code-link: true filters: - ../remove-fmt-skip.lua editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- # Models with numeric explanatory variables ## Mercury and Assets Are mercury concentrations in hair related to household socioeconomic position, as measured by assets? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(tidymodels) library(readr) mercury <- readr::read_csv("../data/mercury_reg.csv") mercury <- mercury %>% # scale() subtracts the mean and divides by the SD to make the units "standard deviations" like a z-score mutate(assets_sc=scale(SESassets)) %>% #another variable we may use later mutate(form_min_sc=scale(FM_buffer)) %>% #so I don't have to remember coding mutate(sex,sex_cat=ifelse(sex==1,"Male","Female")) %>% mutate(native,native_cat=ifelse(native==1,"Native","Non-native")) %>% mutate(hairHg=exp(lhairHg)) ``` ::: ## Goal: Predict mercury from assets $$\widehat{y}_{i} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 \times x_{i}$$ Here $y_i$ represents log hair mercury for subject $i$, and $x_i$ represents standardized household income. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/hg_asset_plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## {background-color="white"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../img/tidymodels.png){fig-align='center' width=98%} ::: ::: ## Step 1: Specify model ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} linear_reg() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Linear Regression Model Specification (regression) #> #> Computational engine: lm ``` ::: ::: ## Step 2: Set model fitting *engine* ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} linear_reg() %>% set_engine("lm") # lm: linear model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Linear Regression Model Specification (regression) #> #> Computational engine: lm ``` ::: ::: ## Step 3: Fit model & estimate parameters ... using **formula syntax** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} linear_reg() %>% set_engine("lm") %>% fit(lhairHg ~ assets_sc, data = mercury) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> parsnip model object #> #> #> Call: #> stats::lm(formula = lhairHg ~ assets_sc, data = data) #> #> Coefficients: #> (Intercept) assets_sc #> 0.2795 -0.3577 ``` ::: ::: ## A closer look at model output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> parsnip model object #> #> #> Call: #> stats::lm(formula = lhairHg ~ assets_sc, data = data) #> #> Coefficients: #> (Intercept) assets_sc #> 0.2795 -0.3577 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.large} $$\widehat{y}_{i} = 0.2795 - 0.3577 \times x_{i}$$ ::: ## A tidy look at model output ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} linear_reg() %>% set_engine("lm") %>% fit(lhairHg ~ assets_sc, data = mercury) %>% tidy() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 2 × 5 #> term estimate std.error statistic p.value #> #> 1 (Intercept) 0.280 0.0213 13.1 7.49e-38 #> 2 assets_sc -0.358 0.0216 -16.5 3.90e-58 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.large} $$\widehat{y}_{i} = 0.280 - 0.358 \times x_{i}$$ ::: ## Slope and intercept ::: {.large} $$\widehat{y}_{i} = 0.280 - 0.358 \times x_{i}$$ :::
::: {.incremental} - **Slope:** For each standard deviation increase in assets, the log hair mercury level is expected to be lower, on average, by 0.358 log ppm. - perhaps not a very useful statement given the scale - **Intercept:** Individuals with household assets at the mean level (`assets_sc`=0) are expected to have hair mercury concentrations of 0.280 log ppm, on average - Remember `assets_sc` was standardized, so `assets_sc`=0 does not mean "no assets" but instead means "average assets" as it corresponds to an assets z-score of 0. :::
## Slope and intercept: easy/standard case Interpretation is a little easier without a log transformation. Suppose our outcome $y$ is exam score, and the predictor $x$ is hours studied, and we fit a linear model and get the following estimated line. ::: {.large} $$\widehat{y}_{i} = 60 + 5 \times x_{i}$$ :::
::: {.incremental} - **Slope:** For each additional hour of study, the exam score is expected to be higher, on average, by 5 points. - **Intercept:** Individuals who do not study are expected to have exam scores of 60 points, on average - Note: now you can see the danger of extrapolating beyond the range of the data. We don't expect someone who studies 20 hours to have an exam score of 160 on a 100-point scale -- at some point, mastery (hopefully not futility!) is reached. :::
# Better Interpretation in Models wiht Log Transformation ## Working with logs - Subtraction and logs: $log(a) − log(b) = log(a / b)$ - Natural logarithm: $e^{log(x)} = x$ - We can use these identities to "undo" the log transformation ## Interpreting the slope The slope coefficient for the log transformed model is -0.3577, meaning the log mercury difference between people whose household incomes are one SD apart is predicted to be -0.3577 log ppm. ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Using this information, and properties of logs that we just reviewed, fill in the blanks in the following alternate interpretation of the slope: >For each additional SD the household assets are greater, the hair mercury concentration is expected to be `___` , on average, by a factor of `___`. ::: ::: ## {background-color="white"}
>For each additional increase in scaled assets, hair mercury content is expected to be `___` , on average, by a factor of `___`. $$ log(\text{hair Hg for assets x+1}) - log(\text{hair Hg for assets x}) = -0.3577 $$ ::: {.fragment} $$ log\left(\frac{\text{hair Hg for assets x+1}}{\text{hair Hg for assets x}}\right) = -0.3577 $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$ e^{log\left(\frac{\text{Hg for assets x+1}}{\text{Hg for assets x}}\right)} = e^{-0.3577} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$ \frac{\text{Hg for assets x+1}}{\text{Hg for assets x}} \approx 0.70 $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} For each SD increase in assets, the hair Hg is expected to be lower, on average, by a factor of 0.70. :::
## Correlation does not imply causation Remember this when interpreting model coefficients ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../img/cell_phones.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: {.footnote} Source: XKCD, [Cell phones](https://xkcd.com/925/) ::: # Parameter estimation ## Linear model with a single predictor - We're interested in $\beta_0$ (population parameter for the intercept) and $\beta_1$ (population parameter for the slope) in the following model: $$y_{i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1~x_{i}+\varepsilon_i$$ where $\varepsilon$ represents random error around our mean ::: {.fragment} - Tough luck, you can't have them... ::: ::: {.fragment} - So we use sample statistics to estimate them, using the notation $b$ or $\widehat{\beta}$ to distinguish our estimates from the true parameters $\beta$ $$\widehat{y}_{i} = b_0 + b_1~x_{i}$$ or $$\widehat{y}_i = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1~x_i$$ ::: ## Least squares regression - The regression line minimizes the sum of squared residuals. - If $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$, then, the regression line minimizes $\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i^2$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/least-squares-illustration-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Visualizing residuals ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/vis-res-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Visualizing residuals (cont.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/vis-res-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Visualizing residuals (cont.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/vis-res-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## How well does the model fit? $R^2$
The **coefficient of determination**, $R^2$, measures the proportion of variation in the response $y$ that is explained by the regression model. $$ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\widehat{y}_i)^2} {\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar{y})^2} $$ - $\sum (y_i-\widehat{y}_i)^2$: variation **not explained** by the model - $\sum (y_i-\bar{y})^2$: **total variation** in $y$ ::: {.fragment} $R^2$ ranges from **0 to 1**. - $R^2 = 0$: the model explains none of the variation in $y$ - $R^2 = 1$: the model explains all of the variation in $y$ ::: ::: {.fragment} For simple linear regression with one predictor: $$ R^2 = r^2 $$ :::
## Properties of least squares regression
- The regression line goes through the center of mass point, the coordinates corresponding to average $x$ and average $y$, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$: $$\bar{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x} ~ \rightarrow ~ \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}$$ ::: {.fragment} - The slope has the same sign as the correlation coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_y}{s_x}$ - $s_x$ is the standard deviation of the explanatory variable $x$, and $s_y$ is the standard deviation of the response variable $y$ - If $y$ varies a lot more than $x$ does (large $s_y$ relative to $s_x$), the slope will be steeper for the same correlation — a small change in $x$ corresponds to a much bigger typical change in $y$ - In our example, $s_x$ is the standard deviation of `assets_sc` (which is 1, since it was standardized), and $s_y$ is the standard deviation of `lhairHg` ::: ::: {.fragment} - The sum of the residuals is zero: $\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i = 0$ ::: ::: {.fragment} - The residuals and $x$ values are uncorrelated :::
# Model checking ## "Linear" models - We're fitting a "linear" model, which assumes a linear relationship between our explanatory and response variables. - But how do we assess this? ## Graphical diagnostic: residuals plot (ppm units) ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/residuals-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Code ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3"} hg_asset_fit <- linear_reg() %>% set_engine("lm") %>% fit(hairHg ~ assets_sc, data = mercury) hg_asset_fit_aug <- augment(hg_asset_fit$fit) ggplot(hg_asset_fit_aug, mapping = aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") + labs(x = "Predicted mercury (ppm)", y = "Residuals") ``` ::: ## Augment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hg_asset_fit_aug ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 2,300 × 9 #> .rownames hairHg assets_sc[,1] .fitted .resid .hat .sigma #> #> 1 1 1.97 -0.837 3.05 -1.08 0.000750 2.77 #> 2 3 1.10 0.197 2.12 -1.03 0.000452 2.77 #> 3 11 5.34 -0.280 2.55 2.79 0.000471 2.77 #> 4 13 1.57 -0.280 2.55 -0.981 0.000471 2.77 #> 5 14 2.02 -0.280 2.55 -0.528 0.000471 2.77 #> 6 15 0.599 -0.280 2.55 -1.95 0.000471 2.77 #> # ℹ 2,294 more rows #> # ℹ 2 more variables: .cooksd , .std.resid ``` ::: ::: ::: ## More on `augment()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(hg_asset_fit_aug) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Rows: 2,300 #> Columns: 9 #> $ .rownames "1", "3", "11", "13", "14", "15", "16", "17"… #> $ hairHg 1.9652, 1.0951, 5.3366, 1.5683, 2.0218, 0.59… #> $ assets_sc #> $ .fitted 3.045165, 2.124332, 2.549503, 2.549503, … #> $ .resid -1.0799648, -1.0292319, 2.7870974, -0.981202… #> $ .hat 0.0007495801, 0.0004516563, 0.0004705556, 0.… #> $ .sigma 2.769771, 2.769779, 2.769252, 2.769787, 2.76… #> $ .cooksd 5.708620e-05, 3.122263e-05, 2.385430e-04, 2.… #> $ .std.resid -0.3901294, -0.3717471, 1.0066782, -0.354402… ``` ::: ::: ## Looking for... - Residuals distributed randomly around 0 - With no visible pattern along the x or y axes ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Not hoping for... ::: {.large} **Fan shapes** ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: (Evidence of non-constant variance in residuals across the range of predicted values) ## Not looking for... ::: {.large} **Groups of patterns** ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: (Evidence of a missing predictor) ## Not looking for... ::: {.large} **Other non-random structure** ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Not looking for... ::: {.large} **Any patterns!** ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## {background-color="white"} ::: {.question} What patterns does the residual plot reveal that should make us question whether a linear model is a good fit for modeling the relationship between mercury (ppm) and assets? ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: # Exploring linearity ## Data: Mercury ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Mercury vs. assets ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Mercury vs assets ::: {.question} Which plot shows a more linear relationship? ::: ::: {.small} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: ## Mercury and Assets, residuals ::: {.question} Which plot shows a residuals that are uncorrelated with predicted values from the model? Also, what is the unit of the residuals? ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w08-02-fitting-interpretation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Transforming the data ::: {.incremental} - We saw that `hairHg` has a right-skewed distribution, and the residuals of that model don't look great. - In these situations a transformation applied to the response variable may be useful. - In order to decide which transformation to use, we should examine the distribution of the response variable. - The extremely right skewed distribution suggests that a log transformation may be useful. - log = natural log, $ln$ - Default base of the `log` function in R is the natural log:
`log(x, base = exp(1))` ::: ## Transformations
::: {.incremental} - Non-constant variance is one of the most common model violations, however it is usually fixable by transforming the response (y) variable. - The most common transformation when the response variable is right skewed is the log transform: $log(y)$, especially useful when the response variable is (extremely) right skewed. - This transformation is also useful for variance stabilization. - When using a log transformation on the response variable the interpretation of the slope changes: *"For each unit increase in x, y is expected on average to be higher/lower by a factor of $e^{\hat{\beta}_1}$."* - Another useful transformation is the square root: $\sqrt{y}$, especially useful when the response variable is a count. :::
## Transform, or learn more? - Data transformations may also be useful when the relationship is non-linear - However in those cases a polynomial regression may be more appropriate + This is beyond the scope of this course, but you're welcomed to try it on your own, and I'd be happy to provide further guidance! ## Aside: when $y = 0$ In some cases the value of the response variable might be 0, and ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} log(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] -Inf ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} The trick is to add a very small number to the value of the response variable for these cases so that the `log` function can still be applied: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} log(0 + 0.00001) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] -11.51293 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} If there are a lot of 0 values for $y$, this trick can be less of a good idea, and you may need to take an alternative approach (e.g., a zero-inflated model). ::: ## Homework (Practice) [**IMS Chapter 7**](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-slr.html#sec-chp7-exercises) - Problem 3 - Problem 4 - Problem 7 - Problem 8 - Problem 12 - Problem 17 - Problem 22 - Problem 23

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
